title: Initiative Measure IL26-638: Participation in Athletics at K-12 Schools

context.text: Citizen initiative to the Legislature brought by the political committee Let's Go Washington, which turned in signatures on January 2, 2026; the group said it had collected 445,187. The Legislature did not act on it, so it was placed on the November 3, 2026 ballot; the Secretary of State certified it on August 21, 2026.

question.text: Initiative Measure No. IL26-638 concerns participation in athletics at K-12 schools. This measure would prohibit students it defines as “biologically male” from competing in certain school athletic activities intended for female students only. It would require verification of biological sex by students’ healthcare providers. Should this measure be enacted into law? Yes / No

summary.text: Per the Attorney General's explanatory statement, the measure would prohibit “biologically male students from competing with and against female students” on sports teams or in individual events designated for female students only, which would generally prevent transgender girls from participating on girls' teams. It would apply to public K-12 schools and to private schools that participate in the WIAA or similar nonprofit organizations. Students wishing to take part in female-only interschool sports would have to provide a form signed by their personal health care provider verifying “biological sex” based on reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels. The Office of Financial Management estimates a one-time cost of about $21,000 to the Superintendent of Public Instruction to update guidance, and indeterminate costs to school districts; no effect on state or local revenue.

measure.yesMeans: Prohibits students defined as “biologically male” from competing in school athletic teams or events designated for female students only, and requires a health-care-provider-signed verification of biological sex to participate in those sports.
measure.noMeans: Leaves current law in place: schools may offer sex-separated teams, and OSPI regulations prohibiting discrimination based on sex and gender identity continue to apply.

argumentsFor.text: Argument for (written by parent and education advocate Alesha Perkins, a high school coach, an Olympic medalist, a pediatrician and others): “Female athletes deserve fair opportunities to build confidence, develop skills, and pursue goals. Let’s protect those opportunities and affirm the hard-fought rights established through Title IX in 1972, which expanded athletic access for women by recognizing the necessity of the female category.”

Argument for: “Students would compete in the category that aligns with their sex, verified during routine, medically necessary primary care recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics. During a private, consented visit, a licensed medical professional would verify sex based on the student’s birth records, medical history and/or a standard, non-invasive physical examination.”

Rebuttal of the argument against (same authors): “IL26-638 doesn’t require invasive or expensive exams. Standard primary pediatric care already verifies sex; transferring that record to sports is sufficient.”

argumentsAgainst.text: Argument against (written by the Washington State Nurses Association president, Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates, the League of Women Voters of Washington, a family physician, a retired school nurse and a girls' wrestling coach): this “poorly written measure would require girls as young as 8 to undergo intrusive medical sex certification as a new part of sports physicals. It bans parents from using birth certificates.”

Argument against: “The WA State Nurses Association, Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates, and doctors warn this measure would subject girls to medically unnecessary, embarrassing, and potentially harmful genital exams.”
Argument against: “This statewide blanket ban to kick 5 - 10 trans girls off school teams will negatively impact all girls, leaving no room for case by case decisions.”

researchNotes: The official voters' pamphlet does not publish a 'a yes vote means / a no vote means' statement for this measure; the yesMeans/noMeans text is derived strictly from the Attorney General's explanatory statement. The pamphlet's for/against statements are written by committees appointed under state law; the Secretary of State states it 'is not responsible for the content of statements or arguments' (WAC 434-381-180). Arguments are quoted from the Whatcom County edition of the voters' pamphlet; the statewide-measure pages (9-22) were compared with the Spokane County edition and are identical, and the Secretary of State publishes no separate English statewide edition. The proponents and opponents disagree about what the verification would involve: the measure's text, as summarized by the Attorney General, allows verification based on reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or testosterone levels. The 445,187 signature figure is the sponsor's own claim as reported by the Washington State Standard; the Secretary of State's certification notice is the authoritative source for ballot status.
